rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of non-elution. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
The maximum CRF is already achieved, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 1 as the benchmark.
Shorten the gradient another grid step to test whether full resolution is maintained at a faster cycle time. Injection 2 still has margin at its limiting pair, with R = 2.54.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF, but its first pair has little resolution margin for further steepening. Test higher temperature at the same gradient to assess whether faster elution and favorable selectivity can be obtained together.
Back off one temperature step after the first pair fell below R = 1.5 at 50 C. This tests whether a modest speed improvement over the fully resolved 40 C method can retain maximum CRF.

Test the shortest gradient with lower temperature to improve the temperature-sensitive first pair and a weaker starting solvent to increase early retention. This explores a faster fully resolved alternative while preserving injection 3 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Reduce the gradient slope while retaining the minimum gradient duration and the temperature favorable to the first pair. The shallower ramp should improve its resolution, while the final hold tests whether the last compound still elutes faster than in injection 3.

Increase the final organic fraction one step to accelerate the last peak, which now elutes during the hold. This tests the resolution boundary of the first pair while seeking a faster maximum-CRF method.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the gradient slope while retaining the stronger final solvent that accelerated the last peak. This tests whether the first pair can recover the small resolution deficit and yield a faster maximum-CRF method.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward one step, preserving the slope that resolved every pair in injection 9. The stronger final solvent should shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention, while testing whether earlier elution preserves the first pair’s resolution.

Shift the gradient window upward another grid step while preserving its slope and temperature. Injection 10 retained full resolution, so this tests a further reduction in late-peak retention without sacrificing maximum CRF.

Shift both endpoints upward one more step to reach the maximum final organic fraction while preserving the successful gradient slope. This should further accelerate the last peak; the first pair remains the resolution constraint to monitor.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step with the shortest gradient and strongest endpoint already selected. This tests whether the narrower gradient window can shorten elution further while preserving full resolution of the early pair.

Use the improved first-pair resolution margin to test one temperature step higher. This may accelerate the last peak while retaining maximum CRF, although earlier runs indicate that heating reduces first-pair selectivity.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to test a narrower, faster elution window at the successful 30 C temperature. Monitor the first pair closely because its approach to the dead-time region may offset the resolution benefit of the shallower gradient.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early-pair resolution and test one temperature step above injection 14. This brackets the thermal resolution limit while seeking a slightly faster maximum-CRF method.

Test whether cooling restores full early-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction that failed at 30 C. This completes the nearby starting-solvent boundary check while retaining injection 14 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

The fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method is now bounded by failures at higher temperature and starting organic fraction. Lower the endpoint one step to test whether a modest increase in retention provides a useful resolution margin while preserving a short, maximum-CRF separation.

Test one step lower in starting organic fraction around the fastest fully resolved method, injection 14. This checks whether moving the first pair farther from the dead-time region offsets the steeper gradient and preserves maximum CRF with a similarly short elution window.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 19 to recover its small first-pair resolution deficit through a shallower gradient. This seeks a nearby maximum-CRF alternative with greater early retention, while injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Cool injection 18 by one step to seek greater first-pair resolution margin while keeping the minimum gradient duration. Maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a potentially more robust alternative to the fastest confirmed method, injection 14.

Test a lower starting fraction at the cooler temperature to assess a short, fully resolved alternative with more early-peak retention. Injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method; this nearby condition may offer more resolution margin.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 21 to test additional first-pair resolution margin with a short final hold. The maximum score is already achieved; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 23 to shorten late-peak retention while using its first-pair resolution margin. This tests another short maximum-CRF alternative without repeating a method; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved condition.

Use the final injection to test a nearby condition expected to retain maximum CRF while moving the early peaks farther from the dead-time region. Injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with CRF 1.000 and the last peak at 2.58 min.
